phases.name: Foundational
phases.title: Dyslexia Definitions and Classifications
phases.description: Definitions, classifications, prevalence, diagnostic criteria, and historical evolution of dyslexia
keyFindings: Dyslexia is predominantly characterized by a core deficit in phonological processing
Reading ability is continuously distributed, making prevalence estimates arbitrary
2025 IDA definition removed unexpectedness language and intellectual functioning as defining components
Different definitions may be required for different purposes (researchers, policy makers, practitioners)
U.S. First Step Act (2018) retains unexpectedness framing
UK Rose Report (2009) conceptualized dyslexia as a continuum
phases.evidenceQuality: High - multiple peer-reviewed sources with strong consensus on core definition
controversies: IQ-discrepancy criteria - no universal scientific consensus
Continuum vs categorical views - continuum has stronger support
Role of cognitive testing in assessment - differing views

phases.name: Etiology
phases.title: Causes of Dyslexia
phases.description: Genetic, neurological, cognitive, and environmental factors contributing to dyslexia
keyTopics: Brain structure differences (gray and white matter)
Cognitive factors (phonological, RAN, working memory, attention)
keyFindings: Heritability estimates range from 40-80% based on twin and family studies
2022 GWAS identified 42 genome-wide significant loci associated with dyslexia
Genetic correlation between males and females is 0.91 (similar etiology)
Low SES exacerbates genetic contribution to dyslexia
White matter differences in arcuate fasciculus and perisylvian network
Hypoactivation in left hemisphere reading networks
Phonological deficit hypothesis remains most supported cognitive account
RAN deficits consistently observed and contribute independently to reading
phases.evidenceQuality: High - large-scale genetic studies, neuroimaging meta-analyses, longitudinal research
controversies: Replication of gray matter findings has been inconsistent
General processing speed deficits are less consistent than domain-specific
Attention deficits - mixed evidence, may be comorbid with ADHD

phases.name: Manifestations
phases.title: Dyslexia Manifestations
phases.description: Cognitive subtypes, working memory, attention, biliteracy, maturational asynchrony, and psychological consequences
keyFindings: Primary difficulties at word-reading level with phonological awareness, decoding, encoding
Distinct from developmental language disorder (DLD)
Working memory deficits particularly pronounced in verbal working memory
Sustained attention and behavioral inhibition deficits (less severe than ADHD)
Learning disabilities emerge from maturational asynchrony among interacting systems
Biliteracy subtypes: associative (both languages) and dissociative (one language)
57% of Chinese children with reading difficulties did not have English difficulties
Key environmental risk factors: maternal education, screen exposure during pregnancy
phases.evidenceQuality: Good - longitudinal studies, meta-analyses, cross-linguistic research
controversies: Whether word reading difficulties are linguistically universal or specific
Role of general cognitive deficits vs domain-specific deficits

phases.name: Theoretical Models
phases.title: Theoretical Models of Dyslexia
phases.description: Phonological deficit, double-deficit, temporal sampling, multiple-deficit models, and developmental frameworks
keyFindings: Phonological deficit hypothesis is most influential and well-supported
Double-deficit hypothesis supported by longitudinal evidence (PA and RAN as distinct causes)
Temporal sampling theory proposes impaired encoding of low-frequency envelope information
Multiple-deficit model gaining support - dyslexia typically results from multiple deficits
Cerebellar theory has mixed empirical support
Orthographic depth affects manifestation (transparent vs opaque orthographies)
Developmental timing framework proposes maturational asynchrony among systems
Additive model of RD-ADHD comorbidity supported by cognitive profiles
phases.evidenceQuality: Good - theoretical models with varying levels of empirical support
controversies: Cerebellar theory - controversial with mixed evidence
Domain-relevance vs domain-specific accounts - theoretical distinction

phases.name: Interventions
phases.title: Intervention Approaches
phases.description: BCI-based interventions, early intervention, and general intervention approaches
keyFindings: Early intervention and remediation are critical for dyslexia outcomes
BCI approaches show potential for improving phonological processing
Brain remains plastic throughout life, allowing intervention at any age
phases.evidenceQuality: Limited - only 3 claims extracted due to many papers lacking proper DOIs/PMIDs
phases.note: Phase 5 research is limited - future work should focus on extracting more specific claims about intervention efficacy

phases.name: Controversies
phases.title: Controversies and Debates
phases.description: Assessment/diagnosis controversies, cross-linguistic debates, policy controversies, and definition debates
keyTopics: Role of cognitive testing in assessment
keyFindings: Delphi definition has unresolved issues (prevalence, cognitive functioning, educator guidance)
No universal scientific consensus on IQ-achievement discrepancy
ICD-11 endorses discrepancy, DSM-5-TR focuses on unexpected attainment
83% agree dyslexic difficulties exist on a continuum (vs 65% for cut-off criteria)
Metsala et al. regard discrepancy definition as 'serious error'
Stealth dyslexia not addressed in current definitions
Unexpectedness framing may be inequitable for economically disadvantaged children
Evidence supports both universal and specific cross-linguistic perspectives
phases.evidenceQuality: Good - recent debates in peer-reviewed literature
phases.status: Ongoing debates reflect complexity and diversity of perspectives

phases.name: Methodology
phases.title: Research Methodology
phases.description: Research design, statistical analysis, genetic methodology, and measurement approaches
keyFindings: Multi-center case-control designs commonly used (e.g., 948 cases, 948 controls)
GWAS uses logistic regression with additive model and genomic control
Polygenic risk scores calculated using clumping and thresholding (C+T) method
Linkage disequilibrium score regression (LDSC) for genetic correlations
PolarMorphism for pleiotropic loci identification
XGBoost machine learning with 5-fold cross-validation
Exploratory factor analysis with promax rotation for factor structure
phases.evidenceQuality: Good - methodological papers describing rigorous approaches
phases.implications: Methodological rigor essential for valid conclusions in dyslexia research

crossPhaseThemes.description: Central role of phonological processing across definitions, etiology, manifestations, and theoretical models
Increasing support for multiple interacting risk factors rather than single deficits
Debate about whether dyslexia exists on a continuum or as distinct categories
How dyslexia manifests differently across languages and orthographies
How dyslexia manifests and changes across developmental stages
Brain structure, function, and neural mechanisms underlying dyslexia
How genetic predisposition interacts with environmental factors
